A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same min-p sampling work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V2 reports original GPQA and GSM8K experiments, a self-consistency analysis, and a human evaluation with 54 retained respondents.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments and adds Llama benchmark results, a second human evaluation, and a structured creative-writing evaluation using an LLM judge.

M1.justification: The core min-p equations and implementation remain unchanged. Appendix D.2 introduces an exploratory min-z variant with a median-centered logit selection rule; it is not incorporated into the reported min-p experiments.

E1.justification: The principal reasoning and creative-writing tasks are retained. Appendix C.3 adds three creative-writing prompts requiring schema-constrained outputs, extending coverage to structured generation. The added Llama models concern experimental configurations; cited EQ-Bench, DeepSeek-R1, and agent-training work do not establish additional original task evaluations.

E2.justification: V3 substantially broadens reported comparisons: Table 7 adds greedy and configurations labeled tfs, quad, and dynatemp to AlpacaEval comparisons; Table 12 evaluates combined top-p/top-k sampling. Table 4 newly reports standard-sampling controls for the original human study, alongside the retained min-p and top-p results.

E3.justification: New benchmark settings cover Llama 3.2 1B/3B and Llama 3.1 8B/70B. The second human study changes the inference engine and reported temperature/truncation ordering, thresholds, recruitment, story presentation, and rating instructions. Appendix C.3 introduces structured generation, randomized blind comparisons, and five judge-rated metrics. These are additional protocols, not evidence that the retained benchmark experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds substantial analyses of low-temperature behavior, combined top-p/top-k sampling, higher min-p thresholds, and greedy decoding comparisons (Tables 10–14). Tables 17–18 analyze temperature and configuration effects in constrained writing. The original entropy/Pareto analysis remains, while v2's full benchmark sweep plots are omitted.

E5.justification: Human-evaluation reporting changes from mean ± SD to mean ± standard error, with condition-specific paired-test annotations. Tables 2–3 newly state approximate standard errors of 1–1.5 percentage points and mark results accordingly. Table 7 identifies a seed1337 configuration, but neither version establishes a general repeated-run protocol or an increase in run counts.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 and the original min-p/top-p human means remain unchanged, but v3 adds extensive model, control, ablation, and evaluation results. Under the new human-study protocol, Table 15 reports temperature-3 quality scores of 5.80 for min-p=0.1 versus 1.23 for top-p=0.9. AlpacaEval metric assignments also change: v2 Table 6 reports 58.12/56.54 for win rate/LC win rate at min-p=0.1, temperature 1.5; v3 Table 7 reports 56.54/58.12. This reversal does not establish a performance gain.

T1.justification: The original min-p mathematical definitions are retained. Appendix D.2 adds explicit threshold and selection-set definitions for Top-Nσ and the proposed min-z variant. No new theorem, proof, or formal guarantee for min-p is supplied.

C1.justification: The central claims about dynamic truncation, high-temperature quality/diversity, and human preference remain. The introduction explicitly broadens the experimental contribution to multiple model families and sizes and extends the practical-impact claim to advanced reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1.

C2.justification: V3 newly diagnoses limitations of the original human study, including sampling-order differences and participants overlooking incoherence. It adds explanations for low-temperature convergence, possible problems with combined samplers, and the diversity cost of higher min-p thresholds, plus an argument against universally optimal greedy decoding. Appendix A.5 also acknowledges false positives behind the earlier adoption estimates.

D1.justification: V3 substantially expands reproducibility documentation: it identifies benchmark inference frameworks and details the original survey's recruitment, compensation, presentation, filtering, and data processing. New evaluations include schemas, constraint libraries, prompts, parameter grids, judge instructions, and logging information. These disclosures extend far beyond v2's implementation listing and general experimental descriptions, although some new study details remain incomplete.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially through connections to Top-Nσ as a successor method, independent replications, greedy-decoding studies, adaptive decoding, reinforcement-learning exploration, and DeepSeek-R1 deployment. These relationships are developed in the reproducibility statement and Appendix D, beyond the largely retained traditional-sampler review. Two earlier Shwartz-Ziv information-theory references are removed.

P1.justification: V3 reorganizes the appendices into implementation, benchmark results, additional evaluations, and applications/future work, moving the original limitations discussion to D.2. It extensively documents the existing human study and revises the evaluation narrative and resource discussion. Much of the core method prose remains recognizable.

P2.justification: V3 retains Figures 1–2 but removes v2 Figures 3–6. It redesigns the human-evaluation table to include controls and statistical annotations, expands the AlpacaEval table with configuration identifiers and output lengths, and adds numerous benchmark, analysis, and evaluation tables. Conference formatting also changes headings, headers, and the author block.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens validation through additional model families and sizes, broader comparisons, and a second human study addressing the reported temperature/truncation-order problem. Detailed protocols and correction of misleading adoption estimates improve transparency. Important reporting problems remain: Table 14 conflicts with underlying benchmark tables, and the second study's sample size is unspecified. Nevertheless, the gains in empirical validation and methodological accountability constitute a substantial overall improvement.
